claims.label: Occasional transport bridges hundreds of miles but not distant continents
claims.statement: Occasional means of transport (sea currents, birds, drift timber, icebergs) suffice to carry organisms across a few hundred miles of sea, between islands or from a continent to a nearby island, but not between distant continents, so the floras of distant continents remain distinct.

operationalizations.text: Quantify floristic similarity (shared native species) and phylogenetic dispersal-event frequencies as a function of over-water distance between islands and continents, testing for a steep distance-decay threshold where species sharing drops near zero between distant continents while remaining substantial across a few hundred miles.

Estimate successful natural colonization rates across ocean distances using island floras, dated phylogeographies, currents, bird movements, and organismal dispersal traits. Test for a steep decline after hundreds of miles and near-zero exchange between distant continents.

Plot floristic similarity against ocean distance and ask whether similarity remains appreciable over a few hundred miles, including continent-to-nearby-island gaps, and falls to the level seen between distant continents. Ready floristic exchange between distant continents would count against the claim.

obstacles: Rare trans-oceanic long-distance dispersal events between distant continents do occur on macroevolutionary timescales, though at rates too low to homogenize continental floras.
Observed disjunctions rarely identify the transport mechanism.
Rare long-distance events are hard to estimate from present ranges.
Human introductions contaminate modern distributions.
Ancient land connections and human transport can produce the same distance decay.
Currents, birds, driftwood, and ice are bundled together and are not separate variables in flora data.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.label: Homologous parts change shape and size but keep the same relative connexions
claims.statement: Within a class, homologous parts may change to almost any extent in form and size but always remain connected in the same order; for example, the bones of the arm and forearm are never transposed.

operationalizations.text: Represent anatomical structures within a class (e.g. tetrapod limb skeletons, vertebrate skulls, arthropod appendages) as anatomical connectivity graphs where nodes are homologous elements and edges are articulations, and test whether topological adjacency order is conserved across species despite orders-of-magnitude variation in element dimensions.

For homologous serial elements across sampled classes, code topology of anatomical connections and test whether order is invariant despite variation in element size and shape. Any well-supported transposition refutes the universal claim.

Represent homologous parts as connectivity graphs and test whether, within a class, adjacency order stays fixed while shape and size vary, using gene expression or developmental identity as the homology criterion. The claim is confirmed if transpositions of connection are absent across tetrapod limbs, arthropod limbs and floral organs, and refuted by well-supported reversals of anatomical order.

obstacles: Element loss, fusion (e.g. fused carpals/tarsals or synsacrum), and homeotic transformations can alter local adjacency counts without transposing the proximal-distal order of remaining elements.
Homology assignments can be disputed after fusion or loss.
No public dataset exhaustively codes connection order across all cited classes.
Homology has often been defined by conserved connections, so a purely anatomical test can become circular.
Connectivity is coded in an ontology for vertebrate anatomy and is not a downloadable comparative matrix for insect mouthparts, crustacean limbs and flowers together.
Digit identity shifts and homeotic floral changes require an agreed homology standard before they count as transpositions.

claims.label: Parts unusually developed relative to congeners are highly variable
claims.statement: A part developed to an extraordinary degree or in an extraordinary manner in one species, compared with the same part in closely allied species, tends to be highly variable within that species; the rule does not apply when the unusual part is shared by a whole group.

operationalizations.text: Across congeneric species, identify traits with unusually large evolutionary divergence or extreme relative size in one species compared to its congeners, and test whether the intraspecific coefficient of variation (CV) or static allometric slope of that trait is significantly higher in that species than in congeners or than non-exaggerated reference traits.

Quantify how exceptional a species' trait is relative to congeners and relate that value to within-species trait variance, distinguishing species-specific from clade-wide novelty. A positive phylogenetically controlled association supports the rule.

Using individual measurements, compare within-species coefficients of variation of traits that are extreme relative to congeners with variation in ordinary traits, and repeat the comparison for traits that are unusual for a whole clade. Higher variation only in species-level outliers would confirm the rule; no elevation, or equal elevation when the whole group shares the trait, would refute the two clauses.

obstacles: Mean-variance scaling (Taylor's power law) requires using dimensionless measures of variability such as the coefficient of variation (CV) or log-transformed variance, and controlling for positive static allometry with body size.
Most comparative trait datasets have too few individuals per species.
Defining an extraordinary degree across heterogeneous traits requires normalization.
AVONET traits are primarily size and shape, not the secondary sexual characters Darwin emphasized.
Individual measurements are often unsexed and unevenly sampled within species.
Cirripedes and most non-bird animals lack a comparable individual-level table.

claims.label: Hive-bee cells form by bees sweeping equal spheres and building at intersections
claims.statement: Hexagonal hive-bee cells result from many bees standing at equal distances from one another, each excavating equal spherical hollows, and building up or leaving unexcavated the planes where these spheres would intersect.

operationalizations.text: Analyze high-resolution 3D micro-CT scans, time-lapse recordings, and geometric measurements of honeybee comb construction from initial spherical/cylindrical wax cups to planar hexagonal walls and rhombic bases, testing whether active wax-gnawing/excavation of intersection planes (Darwin's mechanism) or thermoplastic surface-tension flow of heated wax drives hexagon formation.

Analyze time-resolved imaging and bee trajectories during comb construction for equal spacing, spherical excavation, and wall formation at predicted intersections. Systematic construction by another geometry would refute the mechanism.

Compare observed cell angles, wall curvature, and bee spacing during construction with the geometry predicted by equal spheres whose intersections are built up. A match to those angles and to equal inter-bee distances would support the mechanism; systematic deviation, or construction kinematics that do not sweep spheres, would refute it.

obstacles: Experimental studies show that while bees initially build cylindrical/hemispherical cups spaced equally apart, the transition to flat hexagonal walls with 120-degree angles is also strongly mediated by thermoplastic flow of wax heated by bees' bodies rather than purely mechanical excavation.
The required time-resolved construction datasets are sparse and scattered.
Wax deformation after deposition can obscure initial geometry.
Cell measurements and construction videos are scattered in papers and are not a public comb database.
Wax rheology and local building rules can produce similar hexagons without bees sweeping equal spheres.
Finished-comb geometry does not record the positions bees occupied while building.

claims.label: The hive-bee comb is maximally economical of wax
claims.statement: The comb of the hive-bee is absolutely perfect in economising wax, so natural selection, driven by the saving of wax, could carry comb architecture no further.

operationalizations.text: Compare the surface-area-to-volume ratio of the three-rhombi pyramidal base (Maraldi angle $\approx 109^\circ 28'$) of Apis mellifera cells against alternative space-filling polyhedral cell terminations ( specifically the Weaire-Phelan / Tóth truncated octahedron apex with two hexagons and two rhombi) and empirical micro-CT measurements of real combs; refute 'absolute perfection' if another geometry uses strictly less wax surface area for the same volume.

Measure cell volume, wall area, thickness, mechanical constraints, and wax mass, then compare observed combs with constrained mathematical optima. Any feasible architecture using less wax at equal capacity and strength refutes absolute optimality.

Compute wax volume per unit of cell volume for real combs and for nearby alternative angles and wall thicknesses that bees could build. A match to the calculated minimum supports absolute economy; a feasible geometry that uses less wax refutes it.

obstacles: While mathematically a Tóth truncated-octahedron base saves ~0.35% surface area for thin walls, real comb walls have finite thickness and rounded fillets where mechanical stability and larval fit also matter.
Absolute optimality depends on constraints such as strength, temperature, and construction error.
Centralized large morphometric datasets are lacking.
Empirical wall thicknesses and angles sit in scattered morphometric papers.
Economy of wax is not the only function; strength and brood packing define other optima.
'Could not lead further' depends on which construction constraints are treated as fixed.

roles: 3D micro-CT and geometric morphometric datasets of Apis mellifera comb cell angles, wall thicknesses, and volumes

claims.label: Early embryo death is a frequent cause of sterility in first crosses
claims.statement: A very frequent cause of sterility in first crosses between species is the early death of the embryo, which may be exposed to unsuitable conditions within the mother or the egg or seed.

operationalizations.text: Across interspecific first crosses in birds (galliforms and passerines) and angiosperms that produce few or no viable offspring, partition failure rates between lack of fertilization versus post-fertilization embryonic arrest/seed abortion (e.g., endosperm failure in seeds, early blastoderm/embryo death in bird eggs).

Stage reciprocal interspecific crosses and classify failure as pre-fertilization, embryonic death, later mortality, or adult sterility. Estimate the fraction of first-cross infertility attributable to early embryo death.

Among first crosses that fail, record the fraction in which fertilization occurs and the embryo dies early, versus no fertilization or death at a later stage. A large share of early embryonic death would support 'very frequent'; a minority share would refute that wording.

obstacles: Distinguishing unfertilized ova/ovules from very early zygotic death requires microscopic or histological examination of eggs and seeds rather than simple hatching/germination counts.
Negative and failed crosses are underreported.
'Very frequent' requires representative sampling across taxa.
Most isolation indices do not record the developmental stage of death.
Gallinaceous birds and plants, the groups Darwin emphasized, lack a public stage-of-failure table.
Crosses that produce no visible embryo are easily misclassified.

claims.label: Natural selection turns island herbaceous plants into shrubs and trees
claims.statement: Because trees rarely reach distant oceanic islands, herbaceous plants that colonise them gain an advantage by growing taller, so natural selection often converts insular herbaceous plants first into bushes and then into trees, explaining why islands have trees in orders that are elsewhere herbaceous.

operationalizations.text: Use dated molecular phylogenies and global plant growth-form databases to identify evolutionary transitions from herbaceous continental ancestors to woody shrub/tree habits on oceanic islands (insular woodiness), and test whether oceanic islands have a significantly higher proportion of derived woody species in predominantly herbaceous families (e.g., Asteraceae, Campanulaceae, Echium) than mainlands.

Reconstruct growth-form evolution in island plant radiations and compare transitions from herbaceous mainland ancestors to woody island descendants with mainland controls. Test whether repeated insular woodiness is associated with selection on height and ecological release from trees.

Compare growth form of island endemics with their closest mainland relatives and ask whether shifts from herb to shrub or tree are concentrated on oceanic islands that lacked tree colonists in that clade. Woodiness that arrived already evolved on the mainland would fail the in-situ selection scenario.

obstacles: Multiple selective pressures on islands (such as year-round moderate climate lacking frost, drought resistance, or reduced herbivory) compete with Darwin's taller-stature competition hypothesis to explain why insular woodiness evolves.
Trait coverage is incomplete and some TRY access is conditional.
Woodiness can evolve for drought, longevity, or seasonality rather than competition for height.
Ancestral states and colonization direction can be uncertain.
Ancestral growth form and sister-species pairs are not stored as one global analysis table.
Woody colonists establishing more easily than herbs imitates evolution of woodiness after arrival.
The selection mechanism is stronger than the woodiness pattern alone.

claims.label: Protective colours matching backgrounds are maintained by selection
claims.statement: Seemingly trivial characters such as colour can be shaped by natural selection; colours that match the background, as in green leaf-eating insects and heather-coloured grouse, protect their bearers from predators that hunt by sight.

operationalizations.text: Compare predation rates by visual predators on prey individuals or models that match versus mismatch their natural background substrate across field studies and meta-analytic compilations; lower attack or mortality rates on background-matching phenotypes confirm the claim.

Measure visual contrast between prey and natural backgrounds, then relate contrast to detection, attack, survival and heritable colour variation. Lower detection and higher survival for background-matching phenotypes, together with selection on colour, support the claim.

Score prey colour against the background where the animal is found, and compare attack rates on matching and mismatched forms by visually hunting predators. Higher survival of matching forms would confirm a protective effect of the tint; equal survival after accounting for temperature and sexual signalling would refute it. Open photo and specimen archives support the match, while the survival contrast lives mainly in individual experiments.

obstacles: Human visual assessment of colour matching differs from UV-sensitive avian predator vision, requiring calibrated multispectral or predator-vision-modelled datasets.
Field predation experiments using artificial prey models may not capture behavioural posture and microhabitat choice of live prey.
Predator visual systems differ from human or camera colour spaces.
Published experimental datasets cover selected conspicuous systems.
Predation trials that measure the survival benefit are scattered across papers rather than one open table.
Background matching can serve thermoregulation or sexual display as well as crypsis.
Photographs over-represent conspicuous and diurnal animals.

claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs
claims.label: The Natural System expresses propinquity of descent
claims.statement: The 'something more' than mere resemblance that naturalists seek in the Natural System is closeness of descent, which is the only known cause of similarity among organisms and is partially revealed by classifications.

operationalizations.text: Test whether pre-molecular (morphology-based) Linnaean classifications predict independent neutral molecular phylogenies (e.g. synonymous substitutions or non-coding genomic trees) far better than chance and better than purely ecological/functional groupings.

Compare independently inferred molecular phylogenetic distances with historical and modern classifications and organismal similarity matrices. Stronger agreement with common descent than with non-genealogical similarity schemes supports the empirical content, but cannot establish the philosophical phrase 'only known cause.'

Compare traditional classifications with independently estimated molecular trees and ask whether closeness of descent predicts classificatory grouping beyond raw similarity. The claim is confirmed if classifications recover phylogenetic proximity after phenotypic similarity is accounted for, and refuted if they track overall resemblance or ecological similarity instead.

obstacles: The claim that propinquity of descent is 'the only known cause' of similarity is partly conceptual/explanatory and contrasts with non-empirical creationist ('plan of creation') alternatives.
Modern classifications have largely been revised using phylogenetic data, so historical pre-molecular classifications must be used to avoid circularity.
The 'Natural System' and 'something more' are partly conceptual.
Modern classifications often already incorporate phylogenies, creating circularity.
What naturalists 'seek' in a natural system is a historical intention, not a column in a dataset.
Gene transfer and convergence also generate similarity, so descent is not the only measurable cause.
Many ranks were revised after molecular trees existed, so congruence with those trees is partly by later construction.

claims.label: Large areas produce more, faster-forming and wider-spreading new species
claims.statement: Although small isolated areas can favour new species, modification is generally faster on large areas, and forms produced there, having beaten many competitors, spread most widely and give rise to the most new varieties and species.

operationalizations.text: Compare lineage diversification rates, phenotypic evolution rates, directionality of colonization (continent-to-island vs island-to-continent), and global invasion success between species originating in large continental regions versus small isolated regions or islands.

Compare speciation, trait-evolution and geographic spread rates of lineages occupying large continental areas versus small islands or regions under phylogenetic models. Faster modification, more descendant taxa and broader later ranges from large areas support the claim.

Compare speciation rate, geographic range, and richness of descendant clades between lineages inferred to have originated on large landmasses and those from islands or small regions. Faster diversification and wider ranges for large-area clades would support the claim; equal or higher rates for small-area clades, after clade age and sampling effort, would refute it.

obstacles: The claim bundles three predictions (faster modification on large areas, wider spread of large-area forms, and producing the most new species), which do not always covary—island radiations often show rapid per-lineage morphological modification despite continental species dominating global spread.
Area correlates with habitat heterogeneity and climate stability, confounding pure competitive-superiority explanations.
Area, isolation, habitat diversity and sampling intensity are strongly confounded.
Survivorship obscures where extinct forms originated.
Area, island age, isolation, and collecting effort are entangled.
The place of origin of a clade is often ambiguous once it has spread.
Vertebrates and plants are far better covered than terrestrial invertebrates.
